Angelic Hierarchy
an-JEL-ik HAI-er-ar-kee
noun phrase (angelology)
The question of rank and order among the angels. Scripture refers to various angelic ranks and types (cherubim, seraphim, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers) without providing a complete systematic hierarchy; the elaborate nine-order hierarchy of Pseudo-Dionysius is a later speculative systematization the Reformed tradition treats with caution.

📖 Biblical Definition

The question of rank and order among the angels. Scripture indicates that the angels are not an undifferentiated mass but are ordered in ranks and types, while not providing a complete systematic hierarchy. The biblical data: (1) Cherubim, the angelic guardians associated with God's holiness and throne (Genesis 3:24; Exodus 25:18-22, the cherubim over the mercy seat; Ezekiel 1, 10; the living creatures); (2) Seraphim, the burning ones who attend God's throne crying holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:2-3); (3) Archangels, the chief angels (Michael, Jude 1:9; the archangel's voice, 1 Thessalonians 4:16); (4) the Pauline references to angelic ranks among the principalities and powers: thrones, dominions, principalities, powers (Colossians 1:16; also Ephesians 1:21, principality, and power, and might, and dominion; Ephesians 3:10; 6:12; Romans 8:38); (5) the chief princes (Daniel 10:13, Michael one of the chief princes); (6) the innumerable angelic host (Daniel 7:10, thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him; Hebrews 12:22, an innumerable company of angels; Revelation 5:11). The biblical data thus indicates ranks and types of angels (cherubim, seraphim, archangels, and the various principalities and powers) without providing a complete systematic hierarchy. The elaborate nine-order angelic hierarchy of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite (The Celestial Hierarchy, c. 5th-6th century, arranging the angels in three triads of three orders each: seraphim, cherubim, thrones; dominions, virtues, powers; principalities, archangels, angels) was enormously influential in medieval Catholic theology (Thomas Aquinas, Dante's Paradiso) but is a speculative systematization that goes beyond the biblical data. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical data (the angels are ordered in ranks and types) while treating the elaborate Pseudo-Dionysian hierarchy with appropriate caution as speculative beyond Scripture. The substantive point is that the angelic host is real, vast, ordered, and arrayed in the service of God's glory and the ministry of His people, without an exhaustive systematic hierarchy revealed in Scripture.

ANGELIC HIERARCHY, n. phr. (angelology) The question of rank and order among the angels. Biblical data: cherubim (Genesis 3:24; Exodus 25:18-22; Ezekiel 1, 10); seraphim (Isaiah 6:2-3); archangels (Michael, Jude 1:9; 1 Thessalonians 4:16); the Pauline ranks — thrones, dominions, principalities, powers (Colossians 1:16; Ephesians 1:21; 6:12); chief princes (Daniel 10:13); the innumerable host (Daniel 7:10; Hebrews 12:22; Revelation 5:11). Scripture indicates ranks and types without a complete systematic hierarchy. The nine-order hierarchy of Pseudo-Dionysius (The Celestial Hierarchy, c. 5th-6th c.; three triads) was influential in medieval Catholic theology but is speculative beyond the biblical data; the Reformed tradition treats it with caution.

📖 Key Scripture

Colossians 1:16 — "For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him."

Isaiah 6:2-3 — "Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings... And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory."

Daniel 7:10 — "A fiery stream issued and came forth from before him: thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him."

Hebrews 12:22 — "But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Scripture indicates angelic ranks and types without a complete systematic hierarchy; the elaborate nine-order hierarchy of Pseudo-Dionysius is a speculative systematization the Reformed tradition treats with caution.

expand to see more

Angelic hierarchy as a doctrine is held within the bounds of the biblical data. The principal mishandling is the speculative excess that constructs an elaborate, detailed, systematic angelic hierarchy beyond the biblical data. The nine-order hierarchy of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite (a c. 5th-6th-century author writing under the pseudonym of the Dionysius converted by Paul at Athens, Acts 17:34) arranges the angels in three triads of three orders each (seraphim, cherubim, thrones; dominions, virtues, powers; principalities, archangels, angels); this systematization was enormously influential in medieval Catholic theology (Aquinas devotes substantial attention to it; Dante structures the Paradiso around it) but goes well beyond what Scripture reveals. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical data (the angels are real, vast in number, ordered in ranks and types — cherubim, seraphim, archangels, and the various principalities and powers) while treating the elaborate Pseudo-Dionysian hierarchy with appropriate caution as speculation beyond Scripture. The substantive point is the reality, vastness, order, and ministry of the angelic host in the service of God's glory and the care of His people; the precise systematic hierarchy is not exhaustively revealed, and the believer rests in what Scripture teaches without constructing speculative systems beyond it.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Cherubim, seraphim, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers (Colossians 1:16; Isaiah 6:2-3; Daniel 10:13); ranks and types without a complete systematic hierarchy; Pseudo-Dionysius's nine orders treated with caution.
